==Forks==
{{See also|Bitcoin scalability problem|List of bitcoin forks}}

A [[Fork (blockchain)|fork]], referring to a blockchain, is defined variously as a blockchain split into two paths forward, or as a change of protocol rules. Accidental forks on the bitcoin network regularly occur as part of the mining process. They happen when two miners find a block at a similar point in time. As a result, the network briefly forks. This fork is subsequently resolved by the software which automatically chooses the longest chain, thereby orphaning the extra blocks added to the shorter chain (that were dropped by the longer chain).

===March 2013===
On 12 March 2013, a bitcoin miner running version 0.8.0 of the bitcoin software created a large block that was considered invalid in version 0.7 (due to an undiscovered inconsistency between the two versions).
This created a split or "fork" in the blockchain since computers with the recent version of the software accepted the invalid block and continued to build on the diverging chain, whereas older versions of the software rejected it and continued extending the blockchain without the offending block.
This split resulted in two separate transaction logs being formed without clear consensus, which allowed for the same funds to be spent differently on each chain. In response, the Mt. Gox exchange temporarily halted bitcoin deposits.<ref name="Mtgoxforkchain">{{cite web|last=Karpeles|first=Mark|title=Bitcoin blockchain issue&nbsp;– bitcoin deposits temporarily suspended|url=https://mtgox.zendesk.com/entries/21477395-Bitcoin-blockchain-issue-bitcoin-deposits-temporarily-suspended|publisher=[[Mt. Gox]]|access-date=12 March 2013 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140209083022/https://mtgox.zendesk.com/entries/21477395-Bitcoin-blockchain-issue-bitcoin-deposits-temporarily-suspended | archive-date = 9 February 2014| url-status=dead}}</ref> The exchange rate fell 23% to $37 on the Mt. Gox exchange but rose most of the way back to its prior level of $48.<ref name="ArsFork">{{cite web|last=Lee|first=Timothy|title=Major glitch in Bitcoin network sparks sell-off; price temporarily falls 23%|url=https://arstechnica.com/business/2013/03/major-glitch-in-bitcoin-network-sparks-sell-off-price-temporarily-falls-23/|publisher=Ars Technica|date=12 March 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130420050926/http://arstechnica.com/business/2013/03/major-glitch-in-bitcoin-network-sparks-sell-off-price-temporarily-falls-23/|archive-date=20 April 2013|url-status=live|access-date=14 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="VergeFork">{{cite web|last=Blagdon|first=Jeff|title=Technical problems cause Bitcoin to plummet from record high, Mt. Gox suspends deposits|url=https://www.theverge.com/2013/3/12/4092898/technical-problems-cause-bitcoin-to-plummet-from-record-high|publisher=The Verge|date=12 March 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130420073538/http://www.theverge.com/2013/3/12/4092898/technical-problems-cause-bitcoin-to-plummet-from-record-high|archive-date=20 April 2013|url-status=live|access-date=21 March 2018}}</ref> Miners resolved the split by downgrading to version 0.7, putting them back on track with the canonical blockchain. User funds largely remained unaffected and were available when network consensus was restored.<ref name="ChainFork1">{{cite web|title=11/12 March 2013 Chain Fork Information|url=http://bitcoin.org/chainfork.html|publisher=Bitcoin Project|access-date=12 March 2013 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140214122619/https://bitcoin.org/chainfork.html | archive-date = 14 February 2014| url-status=live}}</ref> The network reached consensus and continued to operate as normal a few hours after the split.<ref>{{cite web|title=Bitcoin software bug has been rapidly resolved|url=http://ecurrency.ec/2013/03/bitcoin-bug-resolved/|publisher=ecurrency|date=12 March 2013 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140331083442/http://ecurrency.ec/2013/03/bitcoin-bug-resolved/ | archive-date = 31 March 2014| url-status=live}}</ref>

===August 2017===
Before 1 August 2017, bitcoin users followed a common set of protocol rules.<ref name="nyt-split">{{Cite news
 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/07/25/business/dealbook/bitcoin-cash-split.html
 |title=Some Bitcoin Backers Are Defecting to Create a Rival Currency
 |last=Popper
 |first=Nathaniel
 |date=25 July 2017
 |work=The New York Times
 |access-date=28 July 2017
 |language=en-US
 |issn=0362-4331
}}</ref> On 1 August 2017, bitcoin split into two chains: the Bitcoin (BTC) chain, with a 1 MB block-size limit, and the [[Bitcoin Cash]] (BCH) chain, with an 8 MB block-size limit. The split has been called the ''Bitcoin Cash hard fork''.<ref name="split">{{cite news
 |last1=Smith
 |first1=Jake
 |title=The Bitcoin Cash Hard Fork Will Show Us Which Coin Is Best
 |url=http://fortune.com/2017/08/11/bitcoin-cash-hard-fork-price-date-why/
 |access-date=13 August 2017
 |work=Fortune
 |date=11 August 2017
}}</ref>

[[Segregated Witness]] was also implemented on the Bitcoin chain through a soft fork during the same month.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

== Taxation and regulation ==
{{See also|Legality of bitcoin by country or territory}}

=== 2012 ===
In 2012, the Cryptocurrency Legal Advocacy Group (CLAG) stressed the importance for taxpayers to determine whether taxes are due on a bitcoin-related transaction based on whether one has experienced a "[[Revenue recognition|realization]] event": when a taxpayer has provided a service in exchange for bitcoins, a realization event has probably occurred and any gain or loss would likely be calculated using fair market values for the service provided."<ref name="BitCoin Tax issues Oct 2012">{{cite journal |last1=Stewart |first1=David D. |last2=Soong Johnston |first2=Stephanie D. |date=29 October 2012 |title=2012 TNT 209-4 News Analysis: Virtual Currency: A New Worry for Tax Administrators? |journal=Tax Notes Today |volume=2012 TNT 209-4}}</ref> In April 2012 the FBI acknowledged Bitcoin's potential for illicit use in an internal assessment. The report identified Bitcoin’s decentralized and pseudonymous design as a challenge for law enforcement, noting early signs of adoption by cybercriminals despite limited evidence of widespread misuse. Although it warned of high theft risks via malware and wallet exploitation, it concluded only with ''low confidence'' that, "based on current user and vendor acceptance, that malicious actors will exploit Bitcoin to launder money". The report highlighted third-party exchanges as regulatory choke points under U.S. law, marking one of the first federal acknowledgments of the systemic enforcement difficulties posed by cryptocurrencies.<ref>[https://cryptome.org/2012/05/fbi-bitcoin.pdf "Bitcoin Virtual Currency: Unique Features Present Distinct Challenges for Deterring Illicit Activity"] (PDF). Federal Bureau of Investigation. 24 April 2012.</ref> In its October 2012 study, ''Virtual currency schemes'', the [[European Central Bank]] concluded that the growth of virtual currencies will continue, and, given the currencies' inherent price instability, lack of close regulation, and risk of illegal uses by anonymous users, the Bank warned that periodic examination of developments would be necessary to reassess risks.<ref name="ECBank201210">{{cite web |date=October 2012 |title=Virtual Currency Schemes |url=http://www.ecb.int/pub/pdf/other/virtualcurrencyschemes201210en.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130228022032/http://www.ecb.int/pub/pdf/other/virtualcurrencyschemes201210en.pdf |archive-date=28 February 2013 |publisher=European Central Bank}}</ref>

=== 2013 ===
On 18 March 2013, the [[Financial Crimes Enforcement Network]] (or FinCEN), a bureau of the [[United States Department of the Treasury]], issued a report regarding [[centralized]] and decentralized "virtual currencies" and their legal status within "[[money services business]]" (MSB) and [[Bank Secrecy Act]] regulations.<ref name="FinCEN1" /><ref name="ABA FINCEN" /> It classified digital currencies and other digital payment systems such as bitcoin as "[[Virtual currency|virtual currencies]]" because they are not [[legal tender]] under any sovereign [[jurisdiction (area)|jurisdiction]]. FinCEN cleared American users of bitcoin of legal obligations<ref name="ABA FINCEN" /> by saying, "A user of virtual currency is not an MSB under FinCEN's regulations and therefore is not subject to MSB registration, reporting, and recordkeeping regulations." However, it held that American entities who generate "virtual currency" such as bitcoins are money transmitters or MSBs if they sell their generated currency for [[national currency]]: "...a person that creates units of convertible virtual currency and sells those units to another person for real currency or its equivalent is engaged in transmission to another location and is a money transmitter." This specifically extends to "miners" of the bitcoin currency who may have to register as MSBs and abide by the legal requirements of being a money transmitter if they sell their generated bitcoins for [[national currency]] and are within the United States.<ref name="ArsFinCEN" /> Since FinCEN issued this guidance, dozens of virtual currency exchangers and administrators have registered with FinCEN, and FinCEN is receiving an increasing number of [[suspicious activity report]]s (SARs) from these entities.<ref>{{cite web |date=18 March 2014 |title=Remarks From Under Secretary of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence David S. Cohen on 'Addressing the Illicit Finance Risks of Virtual Currency' |url=http://www.treasury.gov/press-center/press-releases/Pages/jl236.aspx |publisher=[[United States Department of the Treasury]]}}</ref>

Additionally, FinCEN claimed regulation over American entities that manage bitcoins in a [[payment processor]] setting or as an exchanger: "In addition, a person is an exchanger and a money transmitter if the person accepts such de-centralized convertible virtual currency from one person and transmits it to another person as part of the acceptance and transfer of currency, funds, or other value that substitutes for currency."<ref name="Finextra1" /><ref name="FinCEN1" /> In summary, FinCEN's decision would require bitcoin exchanges where bitcoins are traded for traditional currencies to disclose large transactions and suspicious activity, comply with [[money laundering]] regulations, and collect information about their customers as traditional [[financial institutions]] are required to do.<ref name="ABA FINCEN" /><ref name="JapanTimes">{{cite news |last1=Faiola |first1=Anthony |last2=Farnam |first2=T.W. |date=4 April 2013 |title=The rise of the bitcoin: Virtual gold or cyber-bubble? |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/europe/the-rise-of-the-bitcoin-virtual-gold-or-cyber-bubble/2013/04/04/8be37506-9d34-11e2-9219-51eb8387e8f1_story.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029195258/http://articles.washingtonpost.com/2013-04-04/world/38280106_1_bitcoin-satoshi-nakamoto-monetary-policy |archive-date=29 October 2013 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}}</ref> Jennifer Shasky Calvery, the director of FinCEN said, "Virtual currencies are subject to the same rules as other currencies. ... Basic money-services business rules apply here."<ref name="ABA FINCEN" />

In June 2013, Bitcoin Foundation board member Jon Matonis wrote in ''Forbes'' that he received a warning letter from the [[California Department of Financial Institutions]] accusing the foundation of unlicensed money transmission. Matonis denied that the foundation is engaged in money transmission and said he viewed the case as "an opportunity to educate state regulators."<ref name="NBCnews20130624">{{cite web |last=Coldewey |first=Devin |date=24 June 2013 |title=Bitcoin losing shine after hitting the spotlight |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/technology/bitcoin-losing-shine-after-hitting-spotlight-6C10066339 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130805035505/http://www.nbcnews.com/technology/bitcoin-losing-shine-after-hitting-spotlight-6C10066339 |archive-date=5 August 2013 |work=NBC News}}</ref> In late July 2013, the industry group Committee for the Establishment of the Digital Asset Transfer Authority began to form to set best practices and standards, to work with regulators and policymakers to adapt existing currency requirements to digital currency technology and business models and develop risk management standards.<ref name="WashPost20130730">{{cite news |last=Tsukayama |first=Hayley |date=30 July 2013 |title=Bitcoin, others set up standards group |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/technology/bitcoin-industry-leaders-set-up-standards-group/2013/07/30/8ce4d73c-f94c-11e2-afc1-c850c6ee5af8_story.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130731123011/http://www.washingtonpost.com/business/technology/bitcoin-industry-leaders-set-up-standards-group/2013/07/30/8ce4d73c-f94c-11e2-afc1-c850c6ee5af8_story.html |archive-date=31 July 2013 |newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref> In August 2013, the German Finance Ministry characterized bitcoin as a [[unit of account]],<ref name="Marketwatch20130819" /><ref name="FAZ20130816">{{cite news |last=Nestler |first=Franz |date=16 August 2013 |title=Deutschland erkennt Bitcoins als privates Geld an (Germany recognizes Bitcoin as private money) |url=https://www.faz.net/aktuell/finanzen/devisen-rohstoffe/digitale-waehrung-deutschland-erkennt-bitcoins-als-privates-geld-an-12535059.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131022100540/https://www.faz.net/aktuell/finanzen/devisen-rohstoffe/digitale-waehrung-deutschland-erkennt-bitcoins-als-privates-geld-an-12535059.html |archive-date=22 October 2013 |access-date=24 November 2013 |website=[[Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung]]}}</ref> usable in [[Clearing house (finance)|multilateral clearing circles]] and subject to capital gains tax if held less than one year.<ref name="FAZ20130816" />

On 5 December 2013, the [[People's Bank of China]] announced in a press release regarding bitcoin regulation that whilst individuals in China are permitted to freely trade and exchange bitcoins as a commodity, it is prohibited for Chinese financial banks to operate using bitcoins or for bitcoins to be used as legal tender currency, and that entities dealing with bitcoins must track and report suspicious activity to prevent money laundering.<ref>2013-12-05, [http://www.pbc.gov.cn/publish/goutongjiaoliu/524/2013/20131205153156832222251/20131205153156832222251_.html 中国人民银行等五部委发布《关于防范比特币风险的通知》], [[People's Bank of China]] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140122192430/http://www.pbc.gov.cn/publish/goutongjiaoliu/524/2013/20131205153156832222251/20131205153156832222251_.html|date=22 January 2014}}</ref> The value of bitcoin dropped on various exchanges between 11 and 20 percent following the regulation announcement, before rebounding upward again.<ref>2013-12-06, [https://www.smh.com.au/business/markets/currencies/china-bans-banks-from-bitcoin-transactions-20131206-2yugy.html China bans banks from bitcoin transactions], [[The Sydney Morning Herald]] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140323102824/http://www.smh.com.au/business/markets/currencies/china-bans-banks-from-bitcoin-transactions-20131206-2yugy.html|date=23 March 2014}}</ref> Also in 2013, the U.S. Treasury extended its anti-money laundering regulations to processors of bitcoin transactions.<ref name="foxnews1">{{cite news |url=https://www.foxnews.com/tech/bitcoin-the-nationless-electronic-cash-beloved-by-hackers-bursts-into-financial-mainstream/ |title=Bitcoin, the nationless electronic cash beloved by hackers, bursts into financial mainstream |work=Fox News |date=11 April 2013| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131107093313/http://www.foxnews.com/tech/2013/04/11/bitcoin-electronic-cash-beloved-by-hackers/ | archive-date = 7 November 2013| url-status=live}}. Fox News (11 April 2013). Retrieved on 20 April 2013.</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://blog.aarp.org/2013/04/11/bitcoin-currency-hackers-make-money-investing-in-bitcoins-scams/ |title=Bitcoin Currency, Hackers Make Money, Investing in Bitcoins, Scams&nbsp;– AARP | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140322212826/http://blog.aarp.org/2013/04/11/bitcoin-currency-hackers-make-money-investing-in-bitcoins-scams/ | archive-date = 22 March 2014| url-status=live}}. Blog.aarp.org (19 March 2013). Retrieved on 20 April 2013.</ref>

=== 2014 ===
In 2014, the [[U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission]] filed an administrative action against Erik T. Voorhees, for violating Securities Act Section 5 for publicly offering unregistered interests in two bitcoin websites in exchange for bitcoins.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Casey|first1=Brian|title=Bitcoin – Is Anyone In Charge?|url=http://www.natlawreview.com/article/bitcoin-anyone-charge|access-date=15 September 2014|work=The National Law Review|date=23 July 2014}}</ref> On 25 March 2014, the [[U.S. Internal Revenue Service]] issued Notice 2014-21, clarifying that for federal tax purposes, virtual currency is treated as property, not currency.<ref>[https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-14-21.pdf "Notice 2014-21: IRS Virtual Currency Guidance"]. (PDF). Internal Revenue Service. 25 Mar 2014.</ref>

=== 2016 ===
In 2016, the [[European Parliament]] began discussions to bring virtual currency exchanges and custodian wallet providers under the scope of the Anti-Money Laundering Directive (AMLD). The proposal was published in July 2016, marking "a significant step in the EU's efforts to combat the laundering of money from criminal activities and to counter the financing of terrorist activities."<ref>[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:52016PC0450 "Proposal for a DIRECTIVE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL amending Directive (EU) 2015/849 on the prevention of the use of the financial system for the purposes of money laundering or terrorist financing and amending Directive 2009/101/EC"]. European Commission, Directorate-General for Justice and Consumers. 5 July 2016.</ref>

=== 2017 ===
By December 2017, bitcoin [[futures contract]]s began to be offered, and the US [[Chicago Board Options Exchange]] (CBOE) was formally settling the futures daily.<ref name="fortune20171212">{{cite news |url=http://fortune.com/2017/12/12/winklevoss-twins-bitcoin-futures/ |title=Winklevoss Twins Say Futures Are Just the Beginning for Bitcoin |author=Bloomberg |work=[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]] |date=12 December 2017 |access-date=12 May 2020}}</ref><ref name="bloomberg20171209">{{cite news |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2017-12-09/bitcoin-futures-trading-brings-crypto-into-mainstream-finance |title=Bitcoin Futures Trading Brings Crypto Into Mainstream |work=[[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg]] |date=9 December 2017 |last1=Urban|first1=Rob |last2=Russo|first2=Camila |access-date=12 May 2020 }}</ref>

=== 2019 ===
By 2019, multiple trading companies were offering services around bitcoin futures.<ref name="bloomberg20190909">{{cite news |last=Leising|first=Matthew |date=6 September 2019 |title=Bitcoin Futures on ICE Grow Nearer With Custody Warehouse Start |work=[[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg]] |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-09-06/bitcoin-futures-on-ice-grow-nearer-with-custody-warehouse-start |access-date=9 September 2019 }}</ref>

==Bitcoin faucets==
{{anchor|Bitcoin faucet}}
A ''bitcoin faucet'' was a [[website]] or [[application software|software app]] that dispensed rewards in the form of bitcoin for visitors to claim in exchange for completing a [[captcha]] or task as described by the website. There have also been faucets that dispense other [[cryptocurrency|cryptocurrencies]]. The first example was called "The Bitcoin Faucet" and was developed by [[Gavin Andresen]] in 2010.<ref>{{Cite news | title = Five years of Bitcoin in one post| url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-switch/wp/2014/01/03/five-years-of-bitcoin-in-one-post/| newspaper = The Washington Post| date = 2014-01-03| access-date = 2016-01-15| issn = 0190-8286| language = en-US| first = Timothy B.| last = Lee}}</ref> It originally gave out five bitcoins per person. The rewards were dispensed at regular time intervals as rewards for completing simple tasks such as captcha completion, or as prizes from simple games. The amount of bitcoin would typically fluctuate according to the cash value of bitcoin. Some faucets also had random larger rewards. To reduce [[Bitcoin mining|mining fee]]s, faucets saved up these small individual payments in their own [[ledger]]s, which would be dispersed as larger payment to a user's [[Bitcoin network#Bitcoin addresses|bitcoin address]].<ref>{{cite web | title = Cracking the Bitcoin: Digging Into a $131M USD Virtual Currency | url = http://www.dailytech.com/Cracking+the+Bitcoin+Digging+Into+a+131M+USD+Virtual+Currency/article21878.htm | author = Jason Mick | publisher = Daily Tech | date = 12 June 2011 | access-date = 30 December 2014 | archive-url = https://archive.today/20130120051306/http://www.dailytech.com/Cracking+the+Bitcoin+Digging+Into+a+131M+USD+Virtual+Currency/article21878.htm | archive-date = 2013-01-20 | url-status = dead }}</ref>

Because bitcoin transactions are irreversible and there have been many faucets, they have been targets for hackers interested in acquiring bitcoins through theft or exploitation. Advertisements were the main income source of bitcoin faucets, with the potential reward in cryptocurrency intended to incentivize traffic. Some ad networks have also paid directly in bitcoin. Faucets typically have a low profit margin. Some faucets have also made money by mining cryptocurrencies in the background, using the user's CPU.{{citation needed|date=March 2024}}

==Theft and exchange shutdowns==
Bitcoins can be stored in a bitcoin [[cryptocurrency wallet]]. Theft of bitcoin has been documented on numerous occasions. At other times, bitcoin exchanges have shut down, taking their clients' bitcoins with them. A ''Wired'' study published April 2013 showed that 45 percent of bitcoin exchanges end up closing.<ref name="Wired.co.UK">{{cite magazine|title=Study: 45 percent of Bitcoin exchanges end up closing
|magazine=Wired UK |url=https://www.wired.co.uk/news/archive/2013-04/26/large-bitcoin-exchanges-attacks|access-date=28 April 2013|quote=© Condé Nast UK 2013 }} Wired.co.uk (26 April 2013).</ref> On 19 June 2011, a security breach of the [[Mt. Gox]] bitcoin exchange caused the nominal price of a bitcoin to fraudulently drop to one cent on the Mt. Gox exchange, after a hacker used credentials from a Mt. Gox auditor's compromised computer illegally to transfer a large number of bitcoins to himself. They used the exchange's software to sell them all nominally, creating a massive "ask" order at any price. Within minutes, the price reverted to its correct user-traded value.<ref>{{cite web|last= Karpeles |first= Mark |title= Clarification of Mt Gox Compromised Accounts and Major Bitcoin Sell-Off |date= 30 June 2011 |url= https://mtgox.com/press_release_20110630.html |publisher= Tibanne Co. Ltd. | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140210071513/https://www.mtgox.com/press_release_20110630.html | archive-date = 10 February 2014| url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date= 19 June 2011 |url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T1X6qQt9ONg |title= Bitcoin Report Volume 8&nbsp;– (FLASHCRASH) |publisher= YouTube BitcoinChannel| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140411015524/http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T1X6qQt9ONg | archive-date = 11 April 2014| url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="mick">{{cite web |last= Mick |first= Jason |title= Inside the Mega-Hack of Bitcoin: the Full Story |date= 19 June 2011 |url= http://www.dailytech.com/Inside+the+MegaHack+of+Bitcoin+the+Full+Story/article21942.htm |publisher= [[DailyTech]] |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130422131626/http://www.dailytech.com/Inside+the+MegaHack+of+Bitcoin+the+Full+Story/article21942.htm |archive-date= 22 April 2013 |url-status= dead |access-date= 24 November 2013 }}</ref><ref>Lee, Timothy B. (19 June 2011) {{cite web |url=https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/news/2011/06/bitcoin-price-plummets-on-compromised-exchange.ars |title=Bitcoin prices plummet on hacked exchange |date=19 June 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120410034832/http://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/news/2011/06/bitcoin-price-plummets-on-compromised-exchange.ars |archive-date=10 April 2012 |url-status=live |access-date=14 June 2017 }}, Ars Technica</ref><ref>Karpeles, Mark (20 June 2011) [https://support.mtgox.com/entries/20208066-huge-bitcoin-sell-off-due-to-a-compromised-account-rollback Huge Bitcoin sell off due to a compromised account&nbsp;– rollback], Mt.Gox Support {{webarchive |url=https://www.webcitation.org/5zZUX7u5V?url=http://support.mtgox.com/entries/20208066-huge-bitcoin-sell-off-due-to-a-compromised-account-rollback |date=20 June 2011 }}</ref><ref name="register1">{{cite news|title= Bitcoin collapses on malicious trade&nbsp;– Mt Gox scrambling to raise the Titanic |url= https://www.theregister.co.uk/2011/06/19/bitcoin_values_collapse_again/|date=19 June 2011 |author= Chirgwin, Richard |publisher= The Register | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140414064124/https://www.theregister.co.uk/2011/06/19/bitcoin_values_collapse_again/ | archive-date = 14 April 2014| url-status=live}}</ref> Accounts with the equivalent of more than US$8,750,000 were affected.<ref name="mick" /> In July 2011, the operator of Bitomat, the third-largest bitcoin exchange, announced that he had lost access to his wallet.dat file with about 17,000 bitcoins (roughly equivalent to US$220,000 at that time). He announced that he would sell the service for the missing amount, aiming to use funds from the sale to refund his customers.<ref>Dotson, Kyt (1 August 2011) {{cite web |url=http://siliconangle.com/blog/2011/08/01/third-largest-bitcoin-exchange-bitomat-lost-their-wallet-over-17000-bitcoins-missing/ |title=Third Largest Bitcoin Exchange Bitomat Lost Their Wallet, Over 17,000 Bitcoins Missing |date=August 2011 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140215180429/http://siliconangle.com/blog/2011/08/01/third-largest-bitcoin-exchange-bitomat-lost-their-wallet-over-17000-bitcoins-missing/ | archive-date = 15 February 2014| url-status=live}}. SiliconAngle</ref>

In August 2011, MyBitcoin, a now defunct bitcoin transaction processor, declared that it was hacked, which caused it to be shut down, paying 49% on customer deposits, leaving more than 78,000 bitcoins (equivalent to roughly US$800,000 at that time) unaccounted for.<ref>Jeffries, Adrianne (8 August 2011) {{cite web |url=http://betabeat.com/2011/08/mybitcoin-spokesman-finally-comes-forward-what-did-you-think-we-did-after-the-hack-we-got-shitfaced/ |title=MyBitcoin Spokesman Finally Comes Forward: "What Did You Think We Did After the Hack? We Got Shitfaced" |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131030060415/http://betabeat.com/2011/08/mybitcoin-spokesman-finally-comes-forward-what-did-you-think-we-did-after-the-hack-we-got-shitfaced/ |archive-date=30 October 2013 |url-status=live |access-date=24 November 2013}}. BetaBeat</ref><ref>Jeffries, Adrianne (19 August 2011) {{cite web |url=http://betabeat.com/2011/08/search-for-owners-of-mybitcoin-loses-steam/ |title=Search for Owners of MyBitcoin Loses Steam |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140404115130/http://betabeat.com/2011/08/search-for-owners-of-mybitcoin-loses-steam/ |archive-date=4 April 2014 |url-status=live}}. BetaBeat</ref> In early August 2012, a lawsuit was filed in [[San Francisco]] court against Bitcoinica{{snd}} a bitcoin trading venue{{snd}} claiming about US$460,000 from the company. Bitcoinica was hacked twice in 2012, which led to allegations that the venue neglected the safety of customers' money and cheated them out of withdrawal requests.<ref>Geuss, Megan (12 August 2012) {{cite web |date=12 August 2012 |title=Bitcoinica users sue for $460k in lost bitcoins |url=https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2012/08/bitcoinica-users-sue-for-460k-in-lost-bitcoins/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140411020847/http://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2012/08/bitcoinica-users-sue-for-460k-in-lost-bitcoins/ |archive-date=11 April 2014}}. the operation was a [[Ponzi scheme]].<ref>{{cite web |last= Jeffries |first= Adrianne |title= Suspected multi-million dollar Bitcoin pyramid scheme shuts down, investors revolt |url= |url=http://blogs.telegraph.co.uk/technology/willardfoxton2/100007836/bitcoin-pirate-scandal-sec-steps-in-amid-allegations-that-the-whole-thing-was-a-ponzi-scheme/ |title=Bitcoin 'Pirate' scandal: SEC | archive-date = 14 April 2014| url-status=dead}}. The Telegraph</ref>

In September 2012, Bitfloor, a bitcoin exchange, also reported being hacked, with 24,000 bitcoins (worth about US$250,000) stolen. As a result, Bitfloor suspended operations.<ref>{{cite news |title=Bitcoin theft causes Bitfloor exchange to go offline |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/technology-19486695 |date=25 September 2012 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140327180044/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/technology-19486695 |archive-date=27 March 2014 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last= Goddard |first= Louis |title= Bitcoin exchange BitFloor suspends operations after $250,000 theft |date= 5 September 2012 |url= https://www.theverge.com/2012/9/5/3293375/bitfloor-bitcoin-exchange-suspended-theft |publisher= [[The Verge]] | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140211180646/http://www.theverge.com/2012/9/5/3293375/bitfloor-bitcoin-exchange-suspended-theft | archive-date = 11 February 2014| url-status=live}}</ref> The same month, Bitfloor resumed operations; its founder said that he reported the theft to FBI, and that he plans to repay the victims, though the time frame for repayment is unclear.<ref>{{cite news|title= Bitcoin exchange back online after hack |url= http://www.pcworld.com/article/2010586/bitcoin-exchange-back-online-after-hack.html?tk=rel_news |date= 25 September 2012 |last= Chirgwin |first= Richard |publisher= [[PC World]] | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140414065717/http://www.pcworld.com/article/2010586/bitcoin-exchange-back-online-after-hack.html?tk=rel_news | archive-date = 14 April 2014| url-status=live}}</ref> On 3 April 2013, Instawallet, a web-based wallet provider, was hacked,<ref name="cutler13insta">{{cite web|last= Cutler |first= Kim-Mai |title= Another Bitcoin Wallet Service, Instawallet, Suffers Attack, Shuts Down Until Further Notice |date= 3 April 2013 |url= https://techcrunch.com/2013/04/03/bitcoin-instawallet/ |publisher= [[TechCrunch]] |access-date= 12 April 2013 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140331085500/http://techcrunch.com/2013/04/03/bitcoin-instawallet/ | archive-date = 31 March 2014| url-status=live}}</ref> resulting in the theft of over 35,000 bitcoins<ref>{{cite web |url=http://blockchain.info/tx/5c265c7f63176a07d8c1a90c336e8faac133e69b95eb29e69026377781ebdd1e |title=Transaction details for bitcoins stolen from Instawallet | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131019155836/http://blockchain.info/tx/5c265c7f63176a07d8c1a90c336e8faac133e69b95eb29e69026377781ebdd1e | archive-date = 19 October 2013| url-status=live}}. Blockchain.info (3 April 2013). Retrieved 20 April 2013.</ref> which were valued at US$129.90 per bitcoin at the time, or nearly $4.6 million in total. As a result, Instawallet suspended operations.<ref name="cutler13insta" /> On 11 August 2013, the Bitcoin Foundation announced that a bug in a [[pseudorandom number generator]] within the [[Android (operating system)|Android operating system]] had been exploited to steal from wallets generated by Android apps; fixes were provided 13 August 2013.<ref name="TheRegister20130812">{{cite web |url=https://www.theregister.co.uk/2013/08/12/android_bug_batters_bitcoin_wallets/ |title=Android bug batters Bitcoin wallets / Old flaw, new problem |last=Chirgwin |first=Richard |date=12 August 2013 |website=The Register |archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/6IwX8oDIN?url=http://www.theregister.co.uk/2013/08/12/android_bug_batters_bitcoin_wallets/ |archive-date=17 August 2013 }} ● Original Bitcoin announcement: {{cite web |url=http://bitcoin.org/en/alert/2013-08-11-android |title=Android Security Vulnerability |date=11 August 2013 |publisher=bitcoin.org |archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/6IwXaL2GC?url=http://bitcoin.org/en/alert/2013-08-11-android |archive-date=17 August 2013 }}</ref>

In October 2013, Inputs.io, an Australian-based bitcoin wallet provider was hacked with a loss of 4100 bitcoins, worth over A$1 million at time of theft. The service was run by the operator TradeFortress. Coinchat, the associated bitcoin chat room, was taken over by a new admin.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.smh.com.au/it-pro/security-it/australian-bitcoin-bank-hacked-1m-stolen-20131108-hv2iv.html |title=Australian Bitcoin bank hacked |access-date=9 November 2013 |work=The Sydney Morning Herald |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131230081207/http://www.smh.com.au/it-pro/security-it/australian-bitcoin-bank-hacked-1m-stolen-20131108-hv2iv.html |archive-date=30 December 2013 |url-status=live}}. Retrieved 9 November 2013.</ref> On 26 October 2013, a Hong Kong–based bitcoin trading platform owned by Global Bond Limited (GBL) vanished with 30 million yuan (US$5 million) from 500 investors.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.zdnet.com/article/hong-kong-bitcoin-trading-platform-vanishes-with-millions/ | title = Hong Kong Bitcoin Trading Platform Vanishes with millions | website = [[ZDNet]] | archive-date= 5 April 2014 | access-date = 18 November 2013 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140405165624/http://www.zdnet.com/hong-kong-bitcoin-trading-platform-vanishes-with-millions-7000023039/ | url-status=live}}</ref> [[Mt. Gox]], the Japan-based exchange that in 2013 handled 70% of all worldwide bitcoin traffic, declared bankruptcy in February 2014, with bitcoins worth about $390 million missing, for unclear reasons. The CEO was eventually arrested and charged with embezzlement.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ex-boss of MtGox bitcoin exchange arrested in Japan over lost $390m|work=The Guardian|date=1 August 2015|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2015/aug/01/ex-boss-of-mtgox-bitcoin-exchange-arrested-in-japan-over-lost-480m}}</ref>

On 3 March 2014, Flexcoin announced it was closing its doors because of a hack attack that took place the day before.<ref>{{cite web |title=Flexcoin&nbsp;– flexing Bitcoins to their limit |url=http://malwarezero.org/2014/03/flexcoin-flexing-bitcoins-limit/ |work=malwareZero |access-date=9 March 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140309230510/http://malwarezero.org/2014/03/flexcoin-flexing-bitcoins-limit/ |archive-date=9 March 2014 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Bitcoin bank Flexcoin shuts down after theft |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-bitcoin-flexcoin-idUSBREA2329B20140304 |work=Reuters |access-date=9 March 2014 |date=4 March 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140309213659/https://www.reuters.com/article/2014/03/04/us-bitcoin-flexcoin-idUSBREA2329B20140304 |archive-date=9 March 2014 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.theregister.co.uk/2014/03/04/bitcoin_bank_flexcoin_shuts_down_after_hackers_strike/ | title=Bitcoin bank Flexcoin pulls plug after cyber-robbers nick $610,000 | work=The Register | access-date=9 March 2014| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140310005219/https://www.theregister.co.uk/2014/03/04/bitcoin_bank_flexcoin_shuts_down_after_hackers_strike/ | archive-date = 10 March 2014| url-status=live}}</ref> In a statement that once occupied their homepage they announced on 3 March 2014 that "As Flexcoin does not have the resources, assets, or otherwise to come back from this loss [the hack], we are closing our doors immediately." Users can no longer log into the site. Chinese cryptocurrency exchange Bter lost $2.1 million in BTC in February 2015. The [[Slovenia]]n exchange [[Bitstamp]] lost bitcoin worth $5.1 million to a hack in January 2015. The US-based exchange Cryptsy declared bankruptcy in January 2016, ostensibly because of a 2014 hacking incident; the court-appointed receiver later alleged that Cryptsy's CEO had stolen $3.3 million. In August 2016, hackers stole some $72 million in customer bitcoin from the Hong Kong–based exchange [[Bitfinex]].<ref>{{cite web|title=All Bitfinex clients to share 36% loss of assets following exchange hack|work=The Guardian|date=7 August 2016|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/aug/07/bitfinex-exchange-customers-receive-36-percent-loss-tokens}}</ref> In December 2017, hackers stole 4,700 bitcoins from NiceHash, a platform that allowed users to sell hashing power.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.facebook.com/NiceHash/videos/2013146182237851/|title=NiceHash|website=www.facebook.com|language=en|access-date=7 December 2017}}</ref> The value of the stolen bitcoins totaled about $80 million at the time.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-42275523|title=Millions 'stolen' in NiceHash Bitcoin heist|work=BBC News |date=8 December 2017|access-date=21 October 2022}}</ref> On 19 December 2017, Yapian, a company that owns the Youbit cryptocurrency exchange in South Korea, filed for bankruptcy following a hack, the second in eight months.<ref>{{cite web|title=A South Korean cryptocurrency exchange files for bankruptcy after hack, says users will get 75% of assets for now|work=CNBC|date=19 December 2017|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2017/12/19/yapian-youbit-exchange-files-bankruptcy.html}}</ref> On 11 November 2022, [[FTX (company)|FTX]] filed for [[FTX (company)#November 2022 crisis and bankruptcy|bankruptcy]] with an estimated $8 billion missing in customer funds.

==Arbitrary blockchain content==
Bitcoin's blockchain can be loaded with arbitrary data. In 2018 researchers from [[RWTH Aachen University|RWTH Aachen University and Goethe University]] identified 1,600 files added to the blockchain, 59 of which included links to unlawful images of child exploitation, politically sensitive content, or privacy violations. "Our analysis shows that certain content, e.g. illegal pornography, can render the mere possession of a blockchain illegal."<ref>{{cite web|author1=Roman Matzutt|author2=Jens Hiller|author3=Martin Henze|author4=Jan Henrik Ziegeldorf|author5=Dirk Mullmann|author6=Oliver Hohlfeld|author7=Klaus Wehrle|title=A Quantitative Analysis of the Impact of Arbitrary Blockchain Content on Bitcoin|url=https://fc18.ifca.ai/preproceedings/6.pdf|publisher=Financial Cryptography and Data Security 2018|pages=6–8|date=2018}}</ref> [[Interpol]] also sent out an alert in 2015 saying that "the design of the blockchain means there is the possibility of malware being injected and permanently hosted with no methods currently available to wipe this data".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.interpol.int/en/News-and-Events/News/2015/INTERPOL-cyber-research-identifies-malware-threat-to-virtual-currencies|publisher=Interpol|access-date=25 March 2020|title=INTERPOL cyber research identifies malware threat to virtual currencies}}</ref>
